selection_reason: There is no prior experiment history, so the main uncertainty is which representation is strongest as a simple baseline. This tests an RNA-only, single-profile scVI setup, which isolates the effect of starting with the most straightforward gene-expression model before introducing multimodality, multiprofile aggregation, or more complex fusion. Under a limited budget, a clean baseline is the best first experiment because it establishes a reference point for all later comparisons and helps determine whether added complexity is actually warranted.

The only completed run is a singleprofile RNA-only baseline with scvi_n200, so there is very weak evidence about the impact of RNA encoder choice or whether the profile setting matters. This experiment keeps the model simple and changes only one key factor: switching to scgpt under the same RNA-only, singleprofile setup. It will clarify whether a stronger RNA representation alone improves validation accuracy/F1, and it is the best use of the next budgeted trial because it isolates an important design choice without introducing multimodal or fusion confounds.

The current evidence is sparse but informative: scvi_n200 substantially outperformed scgpt in the rna_only singleprofile setting, while we have no evidence yet on whether moving from singleprofile to multiprofile helps. This experiment isolates the effect of profile setting by testing scgpt with multiprofile and simple avgpool aggregation, without adding image or fusion complexity. It is the best next use of budget because it directly answers an important uncertainty about whether multiprofile processing can recover performance for the weaker RNA encoder, while keeping the model simple enough to interpret and compare against the completed singleprofile RNA-only runs.

The current evidence suggests RNA matters more than image-only features, and the best RNA-only result so far is scgpt with multiprofile + avgpool (config_003), while scgpt singleprofile performed much worse. However, we do not yet know whether adding the image modality improves on this strong RNA baseline when the rest of the setup is held constant. config_026 tests that directly by keeping scgpt, multiprofile, and a transformer aggregator fixed while switching to a multimodal resnet50 + weighted fusion design. This is the best next experiment because it isolates the effect of adding image information under a strong RNA configuration, giving high-value evidence for whether we should exploit multimodal extensions or stay with RNA-centric models under the limited budget.

The strongest result so far is the RNA-only multiprofile scgpt model with avgpool (config_003, 0.530 accuracy), while multimodal config_026 underperformed, so there is uncertainty about whether image fusion helps at all and whether the prior multimodal failure was due to the specific fusion/aggregation choices. This experiment keeps the promising scgpt + multiprofile setting fixed and changes only the image encoder and fusion/aggregation to a logically stronger multimodal design (imagenet_vit_l with transformer + weighted fusion). It is the best next use of budget because it directly tests whether a higher-capacity image representation plus a different fusion strategy can turn the current best RNA backbone into a genuinely beneficial multimodal model, while isolating the effect of multimodal fusion as much as possible.

The current evidence suggests RNA-only baselines are competitive, but the multimodal results are mixed: the best observed model so far is still RNA-only (config_003 at 0.530 accuracy), while multimodal variants have not clearly surpassed it. We also have no direct test of whether image information alone is useful in this setting, especially with a stronger encoder (imagenet_vit_l). This experiment cleanly tests the value of the image modality by itself under multiprofile settings, helping isolate whether multimodal underperformance is due to poor image signal versus fusion/representation choices. It is a strong use of the next budgeted experiment because it reduces uncertainty about a major design decision and informs whether further multimodal complexity is warranted at all.

Current evidence suggests the strongest completed result is RNA-only with scgpt on multiprofile (config_003, 0.5305 acc), while image-only is poor and multimodal variants have not yet clearly beaten the best RNA-only baseline. What remains uncertain is whether the advantage comes from the RNA encoder itself or from the multiprofile/aggregation setup. This experiment isolates that question by testing scgpt in a multiprofile RNA-only transformer setting, keeping modality count minimal while probing a more expressive aggregator. It is the best next use of budget because it directly compares against the strongest RNA-only result and can clarify whether multimodal complexity is unnecessary or whether the gains are actually coming from RNA representation and profile handling.

Existing evidence suggests scgpt with multiprofile is the strongest RNA backbone so far, and the best multimodal result is config_041 (scgpt + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted), but the effect of fusion/aggregation is still uncertain because multimodal variants have not clearly beaten the best RNA-only model. This experiment keeps the same promising encoders and profile setting while changing only fusion from weighted to concat, which helps isolate whether a different multimodal fusion strategy improves over the current best multimodal setup. Under the limited budget, this is a strong exploitative yet informative comparison because it directly tests a logical extension of the most competitive multimodal line without introducing confounding changes.

Evidence so far suggests scgpt is the strongest RNA encoder in both rna_only (config_003/config_040) and multimodal settings (config_041 vs config_026), but singleprofile multimodal results are still unexplored. This experiment tests whether adding imagenet_vit_l to the best-performing RNA encoder in a simple singleprofile multimodal setup improves over the current RNA-only and multimodal baselines, while isolating the effect of profile setting and avoiding a confounded change in aggregation. It is the best use of the next slot because it directly probes a high-value unresolved question—does multimodality help when the profile setting is simplified—using the most promising encoder evidence with a relatively simple fusion choice.

Existing evidence is strongest for singleprofile multimodal models with no aggregation: config_042 is currently best, and config_001/config_040 show that simple RNA-only baselines are weaker but still competitive, so the main uncertainty is whether the gain comes from scvi_n200 or from adding image information. This experiment tests the same singleprofile, no-aggregation, weighted-fusion setup as the best run but swaps the RNA encoder to scgpt, isolating the effect of representation while holding the rest fixed. Under the limited budget, this is the best next experiment because it is a clean, high-value comparison that can either validate the promising singleprofile multimodal direction or show that the improvement is encoder-specific rather than modality-specific.

There is currently no evidence at all, so the most informative first step is to establish a strong single-modality RNA-only baseline. This tests how much signal is available from RNA alone with a high-capacity encoder (scgpt) under the simplest profile setting, helping clarify whether multimodal/image components are likely to add value. Under a limited budget, a clean baseline is the best use of the next experiment because it reduces uncertainty about the fundamental difficulty of the task and provides a reference point for interpreting all later multimodal designs.

The only completed run is an RNA-only singleprofile scGPT model, so the biggest uncertainty is whether profile setting alone changes performance for the same encoder. config_022 tests the same RNA encoder (scGPT) but switches to multiprofile while keeping the model RNA-only, which isolates the effect of profile setting without introducing multimodal or fusion confounds. This is the best next experiment because it is a clean, high-value comparison under a tight budget and will clarify whether the search should prioritize multiprofile RNA-only models or move on to adding image modality and fusion.

The current evidence shows a clear gain from moving scGPT RNA-only from singleprofile/none to multiprofile/transformer (0.41 -> 0.51 acc), but it is still unclear whether the gain comes from multiprofile itself or from the transformer aggregation. This experiment isolates that question by keeping the RNA encoder and profile setting fixed while swapping transformer for avgpool. It is the best next use of budget because it directly tests a key design choice with minimal confounding, helping determine whether the current improvement is robust or whether simpler pooling can match it.

Existing evidence suggests scgpt with multiprofile RNA and simple avgpool already outperforms the earlier singleprofile and transformer variants, but we have no direct evidence about whether adding image features helps when keeping the strongest RNA/aggregation choice fixed. This experiment tests the most informative next question: does a multimodal transformer-weighted fusion with the best-performing RNA backbone further improve over the best RNA-only baseline, while isolating the effect of adding the image modality under a strong aggregation/fusion design. It is the best use of budget because it explores a high-potential extension of the current lead without changing too many factors at once, and it directly compares against the strongest observed direction rather than testing a weaker or redundant variant.

Existing evidence suggests scGPT with multiprofile RNA-only is strong (config_006: 0.5305 acc), while the current multimodal scGPT+ViT result (config_051: 0.5200 acc) does not yet beat it. This experiment tests a cleaner multimodal extension by keeping the promising RNA encoder and multiprofile setting fixed, but switching to a simpler average-pooling aggregation to see whether the transformer aggregator is the bottleneck. It is the best next use of budget because it isolates one important design choice, directly compares against the strongest RNA-only baseline and prior multimodal result, and could reveal whether multimodal gains require a different aggregation rather than a different encoder or fusion family.

Current evidence suggests multimodal models can help, but the best result so far is still a relatively simple multimodal setup: config_049 (multimodal, multiprofile, scgpt + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool, weighted) with 0.5420 accuracy, while transformer aggregation under the same general family was worse (config_051). The main uncertainty is whether the remaining bottleneck is the RNA representation or the fusion/aggregation design. This experiment keeps the stronger multimodal/multiprofile setting and isolates a key design choice by swapping the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 while keeping the stronger image backbone (imagenet_vit_l) and weighted fusion, with transformer aggregation to test whether a richer sequence-based aggregator helps when the RNA input is simpler. It is the best next use of budget because it directly probes whether gains come from representation versus fusion, and it extends the most promising multimodal direction without changing too many factors at once.

The strongest result so far is config_043 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted), but it is unclear whether the gain comes from the PCA RNA representation or from the transformer aggregation. We already have one useful point for the same representation/image pair with a simpler aggregator in config_049, and for scgpt+imagenet_vit_l in config_051, but we lack a direct comparison of weighted vs concat under the strongest known RNA encoder setting. config_045 keeps the best-performing RNA/image/profile combination fixed and changes only fusion from weighted to concat, which isolates a key multimodal design choice while staying close to the current best region. This is the best use of the next experiment because it exploits the promising multimodal multiprofile direction while still reducing uncertainty about whether fusion mechanism is actually responsible for the observed improvement.

Existing evidence strongly favors pca_n2000 over scgpt for multimodal settings, and avgpool has outperformed transformer within the tested pca_n2000+imagenet_vit_l family (config_045 vs config_043). However, we have not yet isolated whether concat fusion can further improve the best-performing backbone/aggregation combination. This experiment tests that specific extension while changing only one key design choice relative to the current best result, making it the most informative next step under limited budget and a plausible path to further gains.

The strongest results so far come from multimodal, multiprofile models with pca_n2000 and image encoder imagenet_vit_l, and avgpool was especially good (config_045). However, we still lack evidence about whether the image backbone is the main driver of performance or whether the choice was specific to Imagenet-ViT. This experiment keeps the promising multimodal/multiprofile setup and pca_n2000 representation fixed, but swaps in resnet50 while using transformer aggregation and weighted fusion, which is a logical next test to probe image-encoder sensitivity under the same general design. It is the best use of budget because it explores an important uncertainty in a region already shown to be strong, rather than spending an experiment on a clearly weaker or redundant configuration.

Existing evidence suggests the best current direction is multimodal with pca_n2000 RNA and imagenet_vit_l, and avgpool beat transformer under multiprofile (config_045 > config_043). What remains uncertain is whether the gains come from multiprofile aggregation or from the multimodal fusion itself. config_025 tests a singleprofile version of the strongest RNA/image backbone with concat fusion, keeping the encoders fixed while removing the multiprofile aggregation component. This is a good next experiment because it directly isolates the effect of profile setting/fusion near the current best-performing region, and could clarify whether the current best setup is fundamentally strong because of multimodality or because of multiprofile aggregation.

There is currently no evidence at all, so the highest-value first step is to establish a strong unimodal image baseline. This test isolates the effect of image representation and profile setting by using image_only with multiprofile and a modern ViT encoder, without introducing RNA or fusion complexity. Under a limited budget, this is the best next experiment because it provides a clean reference point for judging whether later multimodal gains are real, and it avoids spending the first run on a more confounded, harder-to-interpret configuration.

The only completed result is an image-only multiprofile model, so there is strong uncertainty about whether RNA alone is competitive and which RNA encoder is best. This experiment tests an RNA-only multiprofile scvi_n200 baseline, isolating the value of RNA representation while keeping the profile setting fixed. It is the best next use of budget because it adds a clean, informative comparison against the existing image-only baseline and helps decide whether future effort should focus on RNA, image, or multimodal fusion rather than changing multiple factors at once.

The current evidence is strong that RNA-only with scvi_n200 is a solid baseline (config_027 achieved the best accuracy so far), while image-only is much weaker (config_012). What remains uncertain is whether multimodal fusion can add value on top of the strongest RNA representation, and which fusion choice is most effective. This experiment keeps the RNA encoder and multiprofile setting fixed while adding the image branch with weighted fusion, isolating the effect of multimodality with minimal extra confounds. It is the best next use of budget because it directly tests the most promising extension of the current best-performing direction while still providing informative evidence about whether image data actually helps.

The current evidence suggests RNA-only with scvi_n200 is strongest so far (config_027), while multimodal scgpt+imagenet_vit_l with weighted fusion was notably weaker (config_032). However, that multimodal result may reflect the RNA encoder rather than the fusion/training recipe. This experiment tests a clean extension: keep the strong multimodal, multiprofile, transformer-based setup but swap in the better-performing scvi_n200 RNA representation while retaining imagenet_vit_l and weighted fusion. It clarifies whether the multimodal gap is due to representation choice versus fusion, and it is the best use of budget because it directly probes a high-value unresolved design decision with a configuration that could plausibly improve over the prior multimodal baseline without changing too many factors at once.

The strongest result so far is config_050, which suggests that multimodal with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l and transformer aggregation is a promising direction, but the fusion choice is still uncertain. This experiment keeps the best-performing RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and aggregation fixed while changing only fusion from weighted to concat. It will clarify whether the gain comes from the current fusion mechanism or from the rest of the multimodal stack, making it a high-information, low-confounder next step under the limited budget.

The strongest current evidence is that multimodal models with scvi_n200 and transformer aggregation perform best so far, but the gain over concat is small, so the key uncertainty is whether the advantage comes from aggregation/fusion choices rather than the specific RNA encoder. This experiment tests a logical extension by keeping the promising multiprofile multimodal setup with transformer aggregation while swapping in pca_n2000 and weighted fusion, isolating whether the high performance depends on the encoder or if the broader multimodal recipe generalizes. It is the best next use of budget because it is a focused comparison near the current best region, preserves exploitation of the leading design pattern, and can clarify which component matters most without changing too many factors at once.

Evidence so far strongly favors RNA over image-only and suggests scvi_n200 is a strong RNA representation (rna_only multiprofile scvi_n200 is already 0.650 accuracy, while image-only is much lower). However, the impact of profile setting for RNA-only remains unclear because the best RNA result uses multiprofile and we have no direct singleprofile comparison for scvi_n200. This experiment isolates the profile-setting effect for RNA-only with a simple baseline, clarifying whether multiprofile actually matters for the strongest RNA encoder. It is the best use of the next experiment because it answers an important uncertainty with a low-complexity, non-redundant comparison before spending more budget on additional multimodal variants whose incremental gains over the current best are small.

The strongest results so far come from multimodal multiprofile models with scvi_n200 and transformer aggregation, but the best fusion choice is still uncertain: weighted (0.72499 acc) and concat (0.72071 acc) are very close, and both beat the weaker scgpt/pca variants. This experiment keeps the promising RNA encoder, image encoder, profile setting, and aggregation fixed, and changes only fusion to weighted on the resnet50 branch. It directly tests whether the apparent advantage is robust to the image backbone and whether weighted fusion consistently edges out concat/other fusion choices, making it a high-value comparison under limited budget rather than just another broad search point.

The strongest current result is RNA-only with scvi_n200 in multiprofile (config_027), while multimodal gains are inconsistent: scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer is only slightly better than the best RNA-only baseline, and simpler multimodal variants underperform. This experiment isolates the RNA encoder choice by testing scgpt in the same RNA-only multiprofile setting, letting us determine whether the poor multimodal results are due to the RNA representation itself or to fusion/aggregation. It is the best next use of budget because it is a clean, low-confound comparison against the current RNA-only benchmark and could either uncover a better unimodal baseline or rule out scgpt, guiding later multimodal searches.

The strongest evidence so far is that scvi_n200 with imagenet_vit_l and transformer aggregation is a top-performing multimodal multiprofile setup (config_050), but the fusion choice is still uncertain because concat performed almost the same as weighted in the same regime (config_041 vs config_050). This experiment isolates the effect of fusion by keeping the encoder, profile setting, and aggregation fixed while switching to avgpool+weighted, letting us test whether the transformer aggregator is truly necessary or whether performance is robust to a simpler aggregation path. Given the limited budget, this is the best next step because it directly clarifies a high-impact design decision around the current best-performing family, rather than changing multiple factors at once or revisiting clearly weaker settings.

There is no prior evidence yet, so the best use of the first experiment is to start with a strong but not overly complex baseline that is plausibly competitive. This tests whether a multimodal, multiprofile setup with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, avgpool aggregation, and concat fusion is effective. It is a good first choice because it is a reasonable midpoint between simple image-only/RNA-only baselines and more complex transformer/weighted-fusion variants, giving informative evidence about whether multimodal integration is worth pursuing before spending budget on larger design changes.

The only completed run is a multimodal multiprofile model with avgpool+concat, so evidence is very sparse and we do not yet know whether the main gains come from the RNA encoder, the image encoder, or the fusion/aggregation choice. config_051 is a clean, informative extension that changes the image encoder from ImageNet ViT-L to ResNet50 while keeping the model setting, profile setting, RNA encoder (scvi_n200), and fusion type (concat) aligned with the existing best-known setup. This isolates the effect of image representation under otherwise similar conditions, making it a strong use of the next experiment because it balances exploration and exploitation while avoiding multiple simultaneous changes.

Existing evidence is sparse but informative: config_050 (scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + avgpool + concat) is the best result so far, while config_051 shows that switching to resnet50 and transformer aggregation hurts. This suggests the encoder/fusion may matter, but we do not yet know whether the strong result came from the image encoder, the avgpool aggregation, or the concat fusion. config_005 keeps the best-performing encoders from config_050 and changes only aggregation from avgpool to transformer, directly testing whether the pooling choice is the key factor. It is the best next experiment because it isolates one important design decision, is closely tied to the current top configuration, and can either confirm a promising direction or rule out a plausible source of improvement under limited budget.

Existing evidence suggests the current best setting is multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation and concat fusion (0.7207 acc), while avgpool is slightly worse and the main uncertainty is whether fusion should be improved. This experiment isolates the fusion choice by keeping the strong encoder/profile/aggregation setup fixed and changing only from concat to weighted fusion. It is the best next use of budget because it directly tests a plausible refinement of the best-performing line without confounding multiple design changes, and it could yield a meaningful gain or clarify that concat is already sufficient.

Existing evidence suggests the best-performing direction so far is multimodal with multiprofile, scvi_n200 RNA, and ImageNet ViT-L, but the effect of fusion/aggregation is still uncertain: weighted fusion with transformer aggregation is slightly better than concat/avgpool, yet the gains are small and not well isolated. This experiment tests a clean extension by keeping the promising encoders and profile setting fixed while switching to avgpool + concat, which helps clarify whether the stronger results are tied to the fusion choice or whether simpler aggregation is competitive. Under the limited budget, it is the best next experiment because it directly probes a high-value design decision with minimal confounding and can either confirm the current promising direction or show that the simpler baseline is sufficient.

Existing evidence suggests scvi_n200 with imagenet_vit_l is the strongest family so far (best accuracy 0.724989 with weighted fusion), but we have not isolated whether the image branch still helps when switching the image encoder to resnet50, and results with resnet50 are currently weak/unstable in other settings. This experiment tests a logical extension of the best-performing multimodal setup by changing only the image encoder and keeping the strong scvi_n200 + multimodal/multiprofile design, which clarifies whether the performance gap is due to the image backbone rather than fusion or profile setting. It is the best next use of budget because it exploits the most promising direction while making a clean comparison that reduces uncertainty about the contribution of the image encoder under otherwise favorable conditions.

The multimodal multiprofile baselines are strongest so far, with scvi_n200 + ImageNet ViT-L and weighted/concat fusion reaching the best accuracy (~0.725), while resnet50 variants are consistently weaker. However, we still do not know how much of that gain comes from the image branch versus the multimodal fusion itself. This experiment tests an image-only multiprofile model with ImageNet ViT-L and transformer aggregation, giving a clean comparison against the strongest multimodal setups to isolate the value of adding RNA/fusion. Under a limited budget, this is a high-value uncertainty-reducing test because it can tell us whether the current gains are truly multimodal or whether the image pathway alone is already carrying most of the performance.

The strongest current evidence is that multimodal models with scvi_n200 and ImageNet-ViT-L are competitive, with config_003 giving the best accuracy so far (0.724989) and config_005 close behind (0.720714). However, it is still unclear whether avgpool vs transformer-style aggregation is the key driver, since we have not yet isolated this for the scvi_n200 + resnet50 pair under the same fusion choice. config_038 directly tests that by holding RNA encoder, image encoder, and fusion fixed to the reasonably strong scvi_n200/resnet50/avgpool/weighted-style family, while changing only the fusion/combination choice relative to the best-performing trends. This is a good next experiment because it is a focused, informative comparison that can clarify whether the apparent gains come from fusion strategy rather than encoder choice, and it balances exploitation of a promising multimodal direction with uncertainty reduction under a limited budget.

Existing evidence suggests scvi_n200 with ImageNet-ViT and weighted fusion is a strong direction (config_003 has the best accuracy so far, with config_005 close behind), while changing RNA encoder to scgpt has been weak in the one tested multimodal setting. What remains uncertain is whether the stronger transformer aggregation can further improve the best-performing pca/scvi-style multimodal family without changing the profile setting or fusion mechanism. Config_024 isolates this by keeping a multimodal multiprofile setup and weighted fusion while testing the logical extension of transformer aggregation with pca_n2000 and a lighter image backbone. Under the limited budget, this is a good exploitation-plus-learning choice because it probes a promising design axis that has already mattered in prior comparisons, while still providing information about whether aggregation choice can yield gains beyond the current best region.

The strongest results so far come from multimodal multiprofile models with scvi_n200 and imagenet_vit_l, especially with weighted fusion (best accuracy 0.724989), while pca_n2000 has shown weak performance in a comparable multimodal setting (0.572931 with resnet50/transformer/weighted). What remains unclear is whether the poor pca result is due to the RNA representation itself or the specific fusion/image choices used there. config_004 isolates the RNA encoder by keeping a strong image backbone and the same transformer+concat multimodal template as other tested models, but swapping in pca_n2000. This is a good next experiment because it directly tests the importance of RNA representation with minimal additional changes, helping decide whether to keep exploiting scvi_n200 or broaden search around alternative RNA encoders under a controlled multimodal setup.

No experiments have been run yet, so the main uncertainty is the baseline value of each modality and the effect of profile setting/aggregation under the simplest visual-only setup. This experiment tests an image-only multiprofile model with a strong ViT image encoder and transformer aggregation, providing a clean baseline for how much can be learned from images alone before adding RNA or fusion complexity. It is the best first use of budget because it establishes an informative anchor point and isolates the contribution of image representation and aggregation without confounding multimodal design choices.

The only completed run is image-only with ViT on multiprofile data, giving modest accuracy/F1 and leaving the main uncertainty whether RNA adds value at all. This experiment tests a strong, direct extension: keep the same image backbone and multiprofile setting, add scVI RNA, and use weighted fusion with a transformer aggregator. It is the best next use of budget because it isolates the effect of introducing RNA while holding the image side fixed, and the chosen setup is a plausible high-performing multimodal variant rather than a large jump in unrelated design choices.

The current evidence is strong that multimodal + weighted fusion with an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder can work very well (config_021), but it is unclear how much of that result depends on the RNA encoder versus the fusion/aggregation choice. This experiment keeps the promising image backbone, profile setting, and weighted multimodal setup fixed, and swaps only the RNA encoder to scvi_n200 while changing aggregation to transformer. It is the best next use of budget because it directly tests whether the high performance of config_021 is robust to a different RNA representation and whether transformer aggregation adds value over the simpler setting, without confounding too many design choices at once.

The current best results come from the same multimodal multiprofile setup with scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l, and weighted fusion slightly outperforms concat, but the encoder choice for RNA remains the main uncertainty. This experiment keeps the strongest known image branch and fusion/aggregation pattern while swapping only the RNA encoder to scGPT, directly testing whether a more expressive RNA representation improves on the best baseline. It is the best next use of budget because it isolates one high-impact design choice rather than changing multiple factors at once, and it can either yield an immediate gain or clarify whether scvi_n200 is already the stronger RNA encoding in this setting.

The current best results come from multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation, and weighted fusion slightly outperformed concat on the same backbone. However, evidence is sparse on whether the advantage is specific to scvi_n200 or holds for other RNA encoders, and whether the better fusion choice remains under a simpler avgpool aggregator. This experiment isolates the RNA encoder by keeping the strong image backbone and profile setting fixed while switching only aggregation to avgpool and using concat, giving a clean comparison against the strongest scvi_n200 transformer/weighted runs. It is the best next use of budget because it tests a plausible, informative variant of the leading multimodal family without changing too many factors at once, helping determine whether the gain is driven by the RNA representation or by the fusion/aggregation design.

Existing evidence strongly favors multimodal over image-only, and among the tested multimodal models scvi_n200 with imagenet_vit_l is the current best, but the effect of aggregation is still unclear because transformer and avgpool have only been compared under one fusion choice and differ only slightly. This experiment isolates that question by keeping the strong scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + multiprofile setup fixed while switching aggregation to avgpool and fusion to concat, letting us test whether the near-tied performance is robust to a simpler aggregation/fusion choice. It is the best next use of budget because it targets a high-value uncertainty with a close-to-best backbone, so it can either uncover a better variant or sharpen which design choices actually matter without changing too many factors at once.

Existing evidence suggests scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with multiprofile multimodal fusion is strong, but the role of the RNA representation is still uncertain: scgpt performed much worse, while pca_n2000 has only been tested with weaker image/aggregation/fusion settings. This experiment isolates that question by keeping the strong multiprofile multimodal setup and swapping only the RNA encoder to pca_n2000 with transformer+weighted fusion, which should clarify whether performance is driven mainly by the RNA encoder or by the fusion/aggregation stack. Under the limited budget, this is a high-value next test because it is a logical extension of the best-performing direction while still reducing uncertainty about a core design choice without changing too many factors at once.

Current evidence strongly favors multimodal scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l with multiprofile settings, but fusion choice is still only weakly resolved: weighted (0.724989 acc) is slightly ahead of concat (0.720714 acc), while avgpool has not been tested with this same encoder pair and could reveal whether the gain comes from fusion complexity or just multimodal integration. This experiment isolates fusion under the strongest-performing representation/aggregation backbone already observed, while keeping all other choices fixed. Given the limited budget, it is the best next test because it is both high-probability for strong performance and maximally informative about a key unresolved design decision without changing multiple factors at once.

Existing evidence shows image-only with ViT is very weak, while multimodal scvi_n200 models are strong, but the role of the image encoder itself is still unclear because we have not isolated resnet50 vs imagenet_vit_l under a matched setting. This experiment tests whether switching to resnet50 improves an image-only baseline, giving a clean comparison of image representation without changing modality or aggregation. Under the limited budget, this is a useful uncertainty-reducing test that can clarify whether image encoder choice matters enough to justify further multimodal exploration with resnet50.

Existing evidence shows scvi_n200 is the strongest RNA encoder in multimodal multiprofile settings, but we still do not know how much of the gain comes from RNA alone versus image fusion. This experiment isolates the RNA-only baseline with the same encoder and profile setting, clarifying the marginal value of adding images and giving a clean reference point for multimodal comparisons. Under the limited budget, it is the best next test because it answers a high-value uncertainty with a single-factor change rather than further exploring already well-performing multimodal variants.
